content: This document emphasizes the importance of technical work in the delivery of prosthetics and orthotics services. It encourages national and international stakeholders in the field to use this document as a guide for collaboration and development of technical resources. The document adopts a people-centered approach, placing the needs of prosthetics and orthotics service users at the forefront of establishing, developing, and maintaining high-quality services. It advocates for services that are responsive, effective, and efficient, aiming to maximize the number of individuals who can benefit. This approach enhances personal identity and well-being, while also fostering social interactions with family, friends, and the community, as well as access to education and healthcare. Such support enables individuals to thrive and participate in activities that contribute to an optimal quality of life, both personally and socially. The document is primarily intended for policymakers and program managers responsible for healthcare, welfare, rehabilitation, and prosthetics and orthotics services. However, it is also relevant to a wide range of professionals, including service providers, professional organizations, user groups, training institutions, donor agencies, civil society, and non-governmental and international organizations. The structure of the document aligns with the World Health Organization’s (WHO) health systems strengthening framework, addressing four key areas: policy (including leadership, governance, financing, and information), products (prostheses and orthoses), personnel, and service provision. These areas are explored in two complementary parts of the document, with Part 1 outlining standards and Part 2 providing detailed guidance on planning, implementing, managing, and further developing prosthetics and orthotics services and systems. The document was developed through a collaborative, multi-stage process involving WHO departments, regional and country offices, and external experts. The development process also adhered to strict conflict-of-interest management protocols to maintain transparency and public trust. Prosthetics and orthotics are externally applied devices designed to assist individuals with physical impairments or functional limitations. Prostheses replace absent or deficient limbs, such as artificial arms or legs, while orthoses support or modify the structure and function of the neuromuscular and skeletal systems, such as braces or splints. These devices serve various purposes, including improving mobility, alleviating pain, restoring appearance, protecting joints, and preventing or correcting deformities. They are often required for long-term use but may also be needed temporarily. Prosthetics and orthotics services encompass a range of inputs, including policy, products, personnel, and therapy, to deliver appropriate devices and care. These services are integral to healthcare and rehabilitation, aiming to optimize users’ health and well-being. Timely provision of these services is crucial to restoring function and preventing secondary complications. When combined with other interventions, such as education, skills training, and social support, prosthetics and orthotics services contribute to full participation and inclusion in society. The document highlights the significant benefits of prosthetics and orthotics services, which improve mobility, independence, and quality of life for users. These services enable access to education and employment, reduce healthcare costs, and promote social and economic inclusion. They are particularly impactful in low-income populations, helping individuals escape poverty and stimulating economic growth through job creation and market opportunities. Access to prosthetics and orthotics services is a fundamental human right. However, many countries lack adequate facilities, and only a small percentage of those who could benefit from these services have access to them. Governments and stakeholders must collect data on needs and unmet needs to develop nationwide services and monitor progress. Without access to high-quality prosthetics and orthotics, individuals face greater risks of exclusion, dependence, and poverty, which have significant social and economic consequences. The document concludes by emphasizing the importance of implementing the proposed standards to establish and maintain appropriate systems and infrastructure for prosthetics and orthotics services. It outlines a four-step process for implementation: assessing national systems, identifying priorities, developing a strategic plan, and conducting regular evaluations. The standards aim to guide countries toward achieving universal health coverage and ensuring respect for human rights through equitable access to prosthetics and orthotics services.
